title: The French presidential election, April 2027
deck: A far-right candidate leads the polls at 35-36% six months out, promising to end Ukraine funding and cut France's EU bill, in a country the autumn riots left angry and short of money.

card.headline: France votes on 18 April 2027, and the front-runner wants to defund Ukraine and shrink France's EU bill

keyNumber.label: first-round polling for the National Rally candidate in October 2026

forYou.line: France has committed about EUR 27bn and co-leads the Coalition of the Willing. Plan for a scenario in which Paris steps back from mid-2027.
A record EUR 340bn must be raised in 2027 at about 140 basis points over Germany. Polls and budget votes now move French bonds, so treat election risk as part of the price.
A government hostile to the Green Deal could slow enforcement of the deforestation and carbon-border rules. Do not count on delays yet: the rules start 30 December 2026 and 1 February 2027.
The first round is 18 April and the run-off 2 May. Past run-offs have been won by the anti-National Rally side, but not by a safe margin this time.

effects.text: Campaign framed as order versus austerity after the October riots
Le Pen pledges to end Ukraine funding within six months and cap France's EU contribution at about EUR 5bn
Election risk added to French bonds, already stressed by debt at 119% of GDP
EU leaders race to agree the 2028-2034 budget before French, Spanish, Italian and Polish votes
Kyiv and European capitals plan for a gap in French military and financial support
Budget talks harden: Le Pen calls a pre-election deal anti-democratic, Macron backs a larger budget
Any government must pass a fiscal fix with no stable majority, so cuts stay politically costly before the vote
Meloni and Le Pen split on Ukraine, testing whether Europe's right stays united on Russia
If the National Rally wins: France leaves the lead of the Coalition of the Willing, and Moscow gains leverage in any Ukraine deal
A hostile French government would slow enforcement of the deforestation and carbon-border rules and press for exemptions
Sustained French political risk could shift the euro-area core, with investors treating France as a periphery-style credit

whatHappened: France elects its next president in two rounds. The first is on 18 April 2027, and the run-off between the top two is on 2 May. President Macron cannot run again.

In October 2026 polls, the National Rally candidate leads the first round with 35-36%. The material treats Marine Le Pen as that candidate. Her 2025 criminal conviction put her eligibility in legal doubt, and the sources used here do not settle it. This report calls the party's candidate 'the National Rally candidate' where the point matters.

Le Pen has pledged to end French funding for Ukraine within six months of taking office and to cap France's net EU contribution at about EUR 5bn, down from about EUR 8bn. She also calls the push to agree the EU's next seven-year budget before the French vote anti-democratic. Zelensky answered by saying lives are worth more than the price.
whyItMatters: France is the EU's second-largest economy, a nuclear power and a permanent UN Security Council member. It has committed about EUR 27bn to Ukraine and co-leads the Coalition of the Willing. A change of line in Paris would shift what Europe can offer Kyiv.

The vote lands in a fiscal and social squeeze. Debt is 119% of GDP, France pays about 140 basis points over Germany to borrow, and it must raise a record EUR 340bn in 2027. Moody's reviews the Aa3 negative rating on 23 October. In October, about 550,000 people marched in one day and roughly 2,400 were arrested.

The result also feeds other 2027 decisions: the EU budget, the Green Deal rules (the deforestation law from 30 December 2026, carbon-border certificates from 1 February 2027) and Italy's election, where Meloni backs Ukraine.

winners.why: It leads the polls and benefits when the campaign is about order, living costs and distrust of the state.
A French pullback from Ukraine would weaken European unity and its bargaining position in any peace talks, including the summit Putin is seeking with Trump and Xi.

winners.who: Safe-haven assets such as German Bunds
winners.why: Investors tend to buy them when French political risk rises.

losers.why: The riots and the budget fight leave it with little political capital and no candidate known to lead.
France is a leading supporter. A cut would hit hardest at the EU level and in the Coalition of the Willing.

losers.who: Advocates of a larger EU budget
losers.why: A French government wanting a smaller contribution weakens the case for the 2028-2034 package.

losers.who: Importers facing the deforestation and carbon-border rules
losers.why: Uncertainty over enforcement makes compliance planning harder, and delays could favour firms that did not prepare.

whatsNext: 23 October 2026: Moody's reviews France's Aa3 negative rating.
Before end-2026: EU leaders try to agree the 2028-2034 budget. Slippage past the French vote is possible.
30 December 2026 and 1 February 2027: the EU deforestation rules start for large and medium operators, and carbon-border certificate sales open.
18 April 2027: first round. 2 May 2027: run-off. The new president takes over in mid-May.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely first-round result on 18 April 2027?
options: The National Rally candidate finishes first and reaches the run-off
The National Rally candidate is eliminated in round one
predict.explanation: Our judgement, at roughly 70%, is that the National Rally candidate finishes first, since polls show 35-36% in October. A first-place finish does not guarantee a win: in 2017 and 2022 the National Rally lost the run-off, and in 2024 it led round one of the legislative vote yet finished third in seats. Our odds of a National Rally presidency are about 38%.

timeline.title: Macron dissolves the National Assembly
timeline.detail: The vote that followed left France without a stable majority, a problem that persists in 2026.

timeline.title: Le Pen convicted in an embezzlement case
timeline.detail: The court barred her from running for office with immediate effect and the ruling went to appeal. The sources used for this report do not state the appeal outcome, so her eligibility is treated as unconfirmed.

timeline.title: 550,000 march; about 2,400 arrested
timeline.detail: The nationwide cost-of-living unrest set the terms of the campaign: order versus austerity.

timeline.title: Euronews sets out what a Le Pen victory could mean
timeline.detail: Reporting covers her pledges to end Ukraine funding and cap France's EU contribution.

timeline.title: Polling shows the National Rally candidate at 35-36%
timeline.detail: October polls give the party's candidate a clear first-round lead.

timeline.title: Moody's reviews France's Aa3 negative rating
timeline.detail: A downgrade would raise borrowing costs and strengthen the order-and-fiscal-fix message in the campaign.

timeline.title: EU deforestation rules start for large and medium operators
timeline.detail: A hostile French government could slow enforcement, but the rules apply before the election.

timeline.title: Carbon-border certificate sales open
timeline.detail: The first declaration is due 30 September 2027, after the new president takes office.

timeline.title: First round of the presidential election
timeline.detail: The top two candidates go to a run-off.

timeline.title: Run-off
timeline.detail: The winner takes over from Macron in mid-May.

causes.name: Fiscal squeeze
causes.detail: Debt at 119% of GDP and a record EUR 340bn to raise in 2027 leave little room to buy peace or promise relief.

causes.name: Political fragmentation
causes.detail: No stable majority since 2024. Macron cannot run again, so no incumbent bloc has a clear successor.

causes.name: Distrust of the state
causes.detail: Public services, living costs and policing fuel a vote that rewards parties outside the governing centre.

causes.name: The riots
causes.detail: School blockades became nationwide cost-of-living unrest, with about 550,000 marching on 17 October and roughly 2,400 arrests in one day.

causes.name: Bond stress
causes.detail: A spread of about 140 basis points and the Moody's review make fiscal credibility a campaign issue.

causes.name: Foreign-policy pledges
causes.detail: Le Pen's promise to end Ukraine funding and cap the EU contribution turns a domestic vote into a European one.

causes.name: EU deadlines
causes.detail: Leaders want the 2028-2034 budget agreed before votes in France, Spain, Italy and Poland, so the French campaign collides with EU decisions.

causes.name: Candidate uncertainty
causes.detail: Legal doubt about the party's candidate leaves room for a late switch that would change the race.

stakeholders.name: National Rally candidate (Marine Le Pen in the sources)
stakeholders.wants: A first-round win and a majority in the run-off on order, living costs and a smaller EU role
stakeholders.leverage: A durable first-round lead; no need to defend the record
stakeholders.likelyMove: Call the unrest legitimate anger, blame the government, keep the Ukraine and EU-budget pledges at the centre

stakeholders.name: Emmanuel Macron
stakeholders.wants: A successor from the centre and a passed budget; protect Ukraine support and the EU budget deal
stakeholders.leverage: Powers of the presidency; little remaining political capital
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hard line on violence, keep pushing the EU budget and Ukraine files, stay out of the first round

stakeholders.name: Mainstream centre and centre-right candidates
stakeholders.wants: Make the run-off and win the anti-National Rally vote
stakeholders.leverage: Run-off arithmetic: the vote can still consolidate against the party
stakeholders.likelyMove: Offer order plus a fiscal plan; avoid owning Macron's record

stakeholders.name: The left
stakeholders.role: Opposition, close to the protest movement
stakeholders.wants: A candidate in the run-off; resist austerity
stakeholders.leverage: Street credibility with students and unions
stakeholders.likelyMove: Blame police tactics and budget cuts; risk being tied to the looting

stakeholders.name: Zelensky and Kyiv
stakeholders.wants: Continued French money, weapons and diplomatic cover
stakeholders.leverage: Moral argument ('lives are worth more than the price'); European security stakes
stakeholders.likelyMove: Lobby the French public and other European capitals; seek EU-level replacements for French aid

stakeholders.name: EU leaders and institutions
stakeholders.likelyMove: Push the deal before the votes, accepting that it may slip

stakeholders.name: Bond investors
stakeholders.leverage: The spread, currently about 140 basis points over Germany
stakeholders.likelyMove: Demand a premium until the budget and election outcome are clear

stakeholders.name: Moscow
stakeholders.wants: A weaker European line on Ukraine
stakeholders.leverage: Narrative and summitry, including a proposed summit with Trump and Xi
stakeholders.likelyMove: Welcome the National Rally's pledges and press for a deal while Europe is distracted

sectors.why: A record EUR 340bn must be raised in 2027 while election and budget risk raise the premium over Germany.
Sovereign-linked balance sheets suffer when French debt is sold.
A French pullback would force other states to fill the gap; a mainstream win would keep the current line.
A smaller French contribution and a challenge to the timetable would complicate a larger 2028-2034 budget.

sectors.sector: Importers of rubber, wood, coffee, steel and aluminium
sectors.why: The rules start on schedule, but a hostile French government could press for exemptions and slower enforcement.
Safe-haven flows tend to follow French political stress.

sectors.sector: Retail, hospitality and security in France
sectors.why: Unrest hurts shops, while private security and insurance demand rises.

dailyLife.effect: France pays about 140 basis points over Germany. A weaker bond market can feed into mortgage and loan rates.
About 550,000 marched on 17 October. Expect more transport and public-service disruption around strike and march days before the vote.
Living costs are the campaign's main emotional issue, so price news can move votes.
Coffee, wood, rubber, steel and aluminium importers face new paperwork and costs under the EU rules from 30 December 2026 and 1 February 2027, whatever the French result.
Expect French aid to be a daily campaign argument. Voters may see arms and funding stories tied to it.

scenarios.name: Anti-National Rally consolidation
scenarios.looksLike: The National Rally candidate leads round one but loses the run-off as centre, centre-right and left voters back the other finalist. The margin is closer than 2017 or 2022.
signposts: Run-off polls show the National Rally below 50%
A candidate from the centre or centre-right clearly takes second place
scenarios.effectOnWorld: France stays in the Coalition of the Willing, but the next president inherits a weak fiscal position and a restive street.

scenarios.name: National Rally wins
scenarios.looksLike: Order, living costs and anger at the government carry the run-off. The new president pursues the Ukraine and EU-budget pledges from mid-May 2027.
signposts: Mainstream parties refuse to endorse the rival
Further unrest or a Moody's downgrade before the vote
scenarios.effectOnWorld: France steps back from Ukraine funding, presses for a smaller EU contribution and slows Green Deal enforcement. Bond spreads probably widen.

scenarios.name: Campaign shock changes the field
scenarios.looksLike: A court ruling, a market crisis or a new wave of unrest reshuffles the candidates or the issues before April.
signposts: A late candidate switch at the National Rally
A censure vote or emergency budget
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Outcome becomes harder to read; markets and allies price a wider range of results.

scenarios.name: Left-led surprise
scenarios.looksLike: A left candidate overtakes the centre, reaches the run-off and benefits from the movement behind the protests.
signposts: Unions and students endorse a single candidate
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A spending-heavy programme collides with the debt trap; the bond market reacts sharply.

predictions.text: About 70%: the National Rally candidate finishes first in the first round.
About 85%: the National Rally candidate reaches the run-off.
About 38%: the National Rally candidate wins the presidency on 2 May.
About 70%: EU leaders fail to agree the 2028-2034 budget by 31 December 2026.
About 55%, conditional on a National Rally win: the new government formally ends or suspends French funding for Ukraine within six months. Void if the condition is not met.

actions: Build scenarios for a French government that cuts Ukraine support and seeks EU exemptions, and test supply and contract exposure.
Prepare for the deforestation and carbon-border rules as if there will be no delay; treat any exemption as upside.
Add buffers around French strike and protest days until the vote.
Review contracts with French public bodies for budget-cut and payment-delay risk.
Treat the French election as a priced political-risk event, not a tail risk; watch the spread to Germany.
Track the 23 October Moody's review and the budget votes as markers of campaign momentum.
Do not assume the ECB will step in; officials say intervention is not warranted.
Watch run-off polling from February to April, since first-round leads alone mislead.
Plan travel and childcare around announced strike days.
Consider fixed-rate borrowing if yields stay high and the campaign looks volatile.
Expect living costs to stay at the centre of the debate and treat campaign promises on prices cautiously.
Separate order from grievances: prosecute violence and publish a funded plan for schools and living costs.
Decide whether to seek the 2028-2034 EU budget deal before the vote or accept slippage, and weigh the legitimacy cost of rushing.
Prepare EU-level or coalition fallback funding for Ukraine in case French support ends.
Keep Italy and other 2027 election countries in the planning, since the right's split on Ukraine shapes coalitions.

analogues.whatFollowed: Jean-Marie Le Pen reached the run-off and Chirac won with a large majority; a broad front against the far right worked.
Macron beat Marine Le Pen, by about 66% to 34% in 2017 and about 59% to 41% in 2022. The anti-National Rally margin narrowed.
The National Rally led the first round but finished third in seats after tactical withdrawals; the result left a hung parliament.
A right-wing government took office, kept Italy on the Ukraine and EU line, and showed that a populist right can govern within existing alliances.

evidence.method: Drafted from two listed sources (a Wikipedia poll summary and a Euronews analysis) plus the event summary and the linked dossiers on this app. Poll levels, pledges and EU timetable items come from those materials. Background on past French elections is general knowledge held with high confidence. Scenario probabilities and predictions are estimates and carry low confidence. No run-off polling was available, and candidate identity is uncertain.
